name: Learn: RuntimeClass (sandboxing)
objective: CKS › Minimize Microservice Vulnerabilities (20%). Goal: use RuntimeClass to select a sandboxed container runtime (e.g. gVisor/runsc or Kata) for sensitive workloads, and combine it with capability-dropping + non-root hardening — the microservice-isolation tasks that appear on the CKS.
description: Learn how RuntimeClass lets you run sensitive pods on a stronger-isolation runtime (a gVisor or Kata sandbox) instead of the default runc, step by step — then layer capability-dropping and non-root on top for defence in depth.

questions.title: Create a RuntimeClass
questions.teach:
A **RuntimeClass** is a **cluster-scoped** object (`apiVersion: node.k8s.io/v1`, `kind: RuntimeClass`) that names a container runtime the kubelet can use to run a pod.

**Anatomy of the object**
- **`handler`** (required, **top-level — NOT under `spec`**): a string the node's CRI (containerd/CRI-O) maps to a configured runtime binary. gVisor uses `runsc` (a user-space kernel that intercepts syscalls); Kata runs each pod in a lightweight micro-VM.
- **`scheduling`** (optional): `nodeSelector` + `tolerations` so pods using this class land only on nodes that actually have the runtime (and tolerate their taints).
- **`overhead.podFixed`** (optional): extra CPU/memory the sandbox itself consumes, factored into scheduling/eviction.

**How a pod uses it:** `pod.spec.runtimeClassName: <name>` (covered in the next step).

**Exam gotchas**
- `handler` is a **top-level field**, a classic trap is nesting it under `spec` (there is no `spec`).
- Creating the RuntimeClass object does **NOT** install the runtime — it only declares a name pods can request. The node must have that handler configured separately in the CRI (e.g. a `[plugins."io.containerd.grpc.v1.cri".containerd.runtimes.runsc]` block in containerd).
- If the handler isn't configured on the chosen node, the pod fails to start (events show a runtime/handler error) — the RuntimeClass object existing is not enough.
- RuntimeClass is **cluster-scoped**, so no `-n namespace`; names are unique cluster-wide.
questions.prompt:
Create a cluster-scoped RuntimeClass named `gvisor` whose `handler` is `runsc`.

Target: `kubectl get runtimeclass gvisor` exists and its `.handler` is `runsc`.
questions.hint: RuntimeClass is `apiVersion: node.k8s.io/v1`, `kind: RuntimeClass`, with `metadata.name` and a top-level `handler:` field (handler is NOT under spec). Apply it with `kubectl apply -f -`.
questions.solution:
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: node.k8s.io/v1
kind: RuntimeClass
metadata:
  name: gvisor
handler: runsc
YAML
kubectl get runtimeclass gvisor -o jsonpath='{.handler}'   # runsc

questions.title: Run a pod on that RuntimeClass
questions.teach:
A pod opts into a RuntimeClass via **`spec.runtimeClassName: <name>`** (a pod-level field — it applies to the whole pod, not per-container). At schedule time the kubelet asks the CRI to run the pod with that handler.

**Ways to set it**
- Plain YAML with `spec.runtimeClassName`.
- `kubectl run` has no first-class flag, so inject it with `--overrides='{"spec":{"runtimeClassName":"gvisor"}}'` (pair with `--command -- sleep 3600`).
- Or generate a skeleton (`kubectl run ... --dry-run=client -o yaml`) and add the field.

**Exam gotchas**
- The field is `runtimeClassName` (camelCase) directly under `spec`, **not** inside a container and **not** `runtimeClass`.
- It is **immutable** on a running pod — you must delete and recreate the pod to change it (there's no `kubectl edit` path, unlike a Deployment template).
- If the handler isn't configured on the node, the pod stays `Pending`/`ContainerCreating` or errors; the *spec field* is still what you author and what gets graded.
- A RuntimeClass with a `scheduling.nodeSelector` will also constrain where the pod can land — the pod effectively inherits those node requirements.

In this lab the `runsc` binary is NOT installed on the kind node, so the pod may stay `Pending`/`ContainerCreating`. That's expected — we only validate that you requested the runtime, not that it ran.
questions.prompt:
In namespace `runtimeclass-learn`, create a pod named `sandboxed` (image `busybox:1.36`, command `sleep 3600`) that requests the `gvisor` RuntimeClass via `spec.runtimeClassName`.

Target: pod `sandboxed` has `.spec.runtimeClassName` = `gvisor`. (Do NOT expect it to be Running — the runsc handler is absent on this node.)
questions.hint: `kubectl run` supports `--overrides` to inject arbitrary spec fields: `--overrides='{"spec":{"runtimeClassName":"gvisor"}}'`. Or write the pod YAML with `spec.runtimeClassName: gvisor`.
questions.solution:
kubectl run sandboxed -n runtimeclass-learn --image=busybox:1.36 --overrides='{"spec":{"runtimeClassName":"gvisor"}}' --command -- sleep 3600
kubectl get pod sandboxed -n runtimeclass-learn -o jsonpath='{.spec.runtimeClassName}'   # gvisor

questions.title: Contrast with an un-sandboxed pod
questions.teach:
The whole point of RuntimeClass is **isolation selection per workload**. **The isolation spectrum** - **No `runtimeClassName`** → the node's default runtime (usually `runc`): the container shares the host kernel directly. Fastest, weakest boundary. - **gVisor (`runsc`)** → a user-space kernel intercepts syscalls, so a kernel exploit in the container can't reach the host kernel. Small per-syscall overhead; some syscalls unsupported. - **Kata Containers (`kata`)** → each pod gets its own guest kernel inside a lightweight micro-VM — the strongest boundary, at the cost of VM overhead. Sandbox only the *sensitive* workloads and leave the rest on the default runtime for speed — the two pods should differ in their `runtimeClassName`. **Exam gotchas** - Leaving `runtimeClassName` **unset** and setting it to `""` both resolve to the node's default runtime — they behave identically; just omit the field for "use the default". - RuntimeClass selects the *runtime* boundary; it is orthogonal to (and stacks with) `securityContext`, NetworkPolicy, and Pod Security Admission — defence in depth, not a replacement. - `kubectl get pod

-o jsonpath='{.spec.runtimeClassName}'` returns empty for a default-runtime pod — that empty string is the expected "normal" state here.
questions.prompt:
In `runtimeclass-learn`, create a second pod named `normal` (image `busybox:1.36`, command `sleep 3600`) with **no** `runtimeClassName` (default runtime).

Target: `sandboxed`'s `.spec.runtimeClassName` is `gvisor` while `normal`'s is empty — the two differ.
questions.hint: Just `kubectl run normal -n runtimeclass-learn --image=busybox:1.36 --command -- sleep 3600` (no overrides). Leaving runtimeClassName unset means the default runtime.
questions.solution:
kubectl run normal -n runtimeclass-learn --image=busybox:1.36 --command -- sleep 3600
kubectl get pod normal    -n runtimeclass-learn -o jsonpath='{.spec.runtimeClassName}'   # (empty)
kubectl get pod sandboxed -n runtimeclass-learn -o jsonpath='{.spec.runtimeClassName}'   # gvisor

verification.description: 'sandboxed' uses gvisor, 'normal' uses the default runtime (they differ)

questions.title: Harden the sandboxed pod (defence in depth)
questions.teach:
A sandbox is one layer — combine it with standard **securityContext** hardening for defence in depth. For the sensitive pod here you:

- **drop ALL Linux capabilities** (`securityContext.capabilities.drop: ["ALL"]`), re-adding only what's truly needed with `add: ["NET_BIND_SERVICE"]`, and
- **run as non-root** (`runAsNonRoot: true`, plus a non-zero `runAsUser`).

**Pod-level vs container-level (the key distinction)**
- `spec.securityContext` is **pod-level**; `spec.containers[].securityContext` is **container-level**. When both set the same field, the **container value wins**.
- **Pod-level only:** `fsGroup`, `fsGroupChangePolicy`, `supplementalGroups`, `sysctls`.
- **Container-level only:** `capabilities`, `readOnlyRootFilesystem`, `allowPrivilegeEscalation`, `privileged`, `procMount`.
- **Either level:** `runAsUser`, `runAsGroup`, `runAsNonRoot`, `seLinuxOptions`, `seccompProfile`.

**Other hardening fields worth knowing**
- `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false` (blocks gaining new privs via setuid binaries).
- `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` — remember to mount a writable `emptyDir` for `/tmp` or wherever the app writes.
- `seccompProfile.type`: `RuntimeDefault` / `Localhost` (needs `localhostProfile`) / `Unconfined`.
- `runAsNonRoot: true` vs `runAsUser: 1000`: the former only *asserts* non-root and fails the container at start if the image's user is uid 0; the latter actually *sets* the uid. Use both.

**Exam gotchas**
- `capabilities` and `readOnlyRootFilesystem` **must** go on the container, not the pod — putting them pod-level is a silent no-op/validation error.
- `drop: ["ALL"]` then `add` back the few you need — order of drop-then-add is how you minimise capabilities.
- `runAsNonRoot: true` with an image that only runs as root (and no `runAsUser`) → `CreateContainerConfigError`.
- RuntimeClass is a **pod-level** field; keep `spec.runtimeClassName: gvisor` when you recreate the pod to harden it.
questions.prompt:
Replace pod `sandboxed` in `runtimeclass-learn` so it still requests `runtimeClassName: gvisor` AND its container drops **ALL** capabilities and runs non-root (`runAsNonRoot: true`, `runAsUser: 1000`). Keep image `busybox:1.36`, command `sleep 3600`.

Target: pod `sandboxed` has runtimeClassName `gvisor`, `runAsNonRoot: true`, and its container's `capabilities.drop` contains `ALL`.
questions.hint: Delete and recreate with a YAML that has `spec.runtimeClassName: gvisor`, `spec.securityContext.runAsNonRoot: true` + `runAsUser: 1000`, and the container's `securityContext.capabilities.drop: ["ALL"]`. busybox sleep runs fine as uid 1000.
questions.solution:
kubectl delete pod sandboxed -n runtimeclass-learn --ignore-not-found
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: sandboxed
  namespace: runtimeclass-learn
spec:
  runtimeClassName: gvisor
  securityContext:
    runAsNonRoot: true
    runAsUser: 1000
  containers:
  - name: c
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sleep","3600"]
    securityContext:
      capabilities:
        drop: ["ALL"]
YAML

verification.description: 'sandboxed' keeps gvisor AND drops ALL caps + runs non-root

questions.title: Offer a second runtime (Kata)
questions.teach:
A cluster can expose **several** RuntimeClasses so workloads pick the isolation they need — e.g. `gvisor` (handler `runsc`) for syscall sandboxing and `kata` (handler `kata`) for full micro-VM isolation. `kubectl get runtimeclass` lists them all; each is just a name → handler mapping.

**Design points when offering multiple classes**
- The **RuntimeClass name** (what pods reference via `runtimeClassName`) is independent of the **`handler`** (what the CRI maps to a binary) — you can name a class anything; the handler must match the node config. Multiple classes may even share a handler.
- Use `scheduling.nodeSelector`/`tolerations` per class to pin each runtime to the nodes that actually have it (e.g. only sandbox-capable nodes carry the `runsc`/`kata` binaries).
- Set `overhead.podFixed` per class so the scheduler accounts for each sandbox's real resource cost.

**Exam gotchas**
- Adding a RuntimeClass object is cheap and safe (it declares a choice); whether a node can honour a given handler depends on that node's runtime configuration — an unconfigured handler means pods using it won't start.
- RuntimeClass is cluster-scoped: no namespace, and the two objects here (`gvisor`, `kata`) coexist independently.
- Don't confuse the two strings: `kata`'s class name and its handler happen to both be `kata` here, but they are conceptually separate fields.
questions.prompt:
Create a second RuntimeClass named `kata` whose `handler` is `kata`.

Target: `kubectl get runtimeclass` lists both `gvisor` and `kata`, and `kata`'s `.handler` is `kata`.
questions.hint: Same shape as step 1: `apiVersion: node.k8s.io/v1`, `kind: RuntimeClass`, `metadata.name: kata`, top-level `handler: kata`.
questions.solution:
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: node.k8s.io/v1
kind: RuntimeClass
metadata:
  name: kata
handler: kata
YAML
kubectl get runtimeclass   # gvisor + kata
